name: Sixteen Kingdoms
summary: A period of many short-lived states in northern China founded mostly by non-Han peoples (Xiongnu, Xianbei, Di, Qiang, Jie) after the Jin dynasty lost the north, ending when the Northern Wei reunited it (439).

knownFor.label: Battle of Fei River
knownFor.note: Former Qin defeated by Eastern Jin.

location.value: Northern China and the north-west (the Yellow River basin, the Hexi Corridor and Sichuan at times), north of the Eastern Jin.

terrain.value: The North China Plain, the loess plateau, the Wei River valley around Chang’an, and the dry Hexi Corridor.

climate.value: Continental: cold dry winters, hot summers with most rain in summer.

resources.value: Millet and wheat land, horses and pasture on the northern edge, and Silk Road trade through Gansu.

disasters.value: Constant war, famine, Yellow River floods and droughts.

population.value: Fell sharply through war and flight; northern registers recorded only a fraction of the Han-dynasty population.

urbanisation.value: Capitals such as Chang’an, Luoyang, Ye and Guzang (Wuwei) rose and fell with each kingdom.

disease.value: Epidemics often followed sieges and famines.

migration.value: Many northern Han families fled south to the Eastern Jin; Xiongnu, Jie, Xianbei, Di and Qiang peoples settled in the north.

economicBase.value: Farming of millet and wheat, herding of horses and sheep, and forced labour and resettlement by rulers.

tradeRoutes.value: Silk Road trade through the Hexi Corridor to Central Asia, controlled by the Liang states in Gansu.

wealth.value: Generally poor after war; the Liang states and Former Qin were richer in quieter years.

moneyAndTax.value: Taxes paid mostly in grain and cloth; coins were scarce and little used in many areas.

inequality.value: Ruling peoples and their soldiers above the Han farming majority; captives were often enslaved.

governmentType.value: A series of rival kingdoms, many founded by non-Han leaders who used Chinese-style titles and courts.

keyRulers.value: Liu Yuan (Han Zhao). Fu Jian (Former Qin).

succession.value: Often by coup or murder; many kingdoms lasted only a few decades.

institutions.value: Chinese-style ministries run by Han officials, alongside the rulers’ own tribal armies.

stability.value: Very unstable: kingdoms were founded and destroyed every few years; only Former Qin briefly united the north.

eliteConflict.value: Constant wars between kingdoms and between members of the same ruling family.

armyAndTech.value: Heavy armoured cavalry (both rider and horse in armour) and some of the earliest stirrups.

majorWars.value: The Former Qin invasion of the south was defeated by the Eastern Jin at the Fei River (383).

territoryChange.value: Former Qin united the north (376) but broke up after 383; Northern Wei reunited the north in 439.

alliancesRivals.value: The Eastern Jin dynasty in the south, the Rouran on the steppe, and each other.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; armoured cavalry and stirrups spread in this period.

scienceEducation.value: Kumarajiva translated many Buddhist sutras at Chang’an (401–413); the monk Faxian set out for India from there (399).

openness.value: Open to trade and new ideas from abroad.

communicationTransport.value: Horses, carts and ox-carts on old Han roads; camel caravans in the Hexi Corridor.

religion.value: Buddhism grew fast with royal support (for example the monk Fotudeng at the Later Zhao court); Daoism and Confucianism continued.

languageWriting.value: Chinese was the written language; rulers also spoke Xianbei, Xiongnu and other northern languages.

artsArchitecture.value: Early Buddhist cave temples, including the first caves at Mogao near Dunhuang (traditionally dated 366).

socialStructure.value: Ruling clans and their warriors, Han gentry families who served as officials, farmers, and captives.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the ruler and clan; many rulers claimed to be legitimate Chinese emperors.

dailyLife.value: Most people farmed in fortified villages; many families joined powerful local lords for protection.

neighbours.value: The Eastern Jin to the south, the Rouran to the north, Tibetan and Qiang peoples to the west, Goguryeo to the north-east.

ideasReligions.value: Buddhism spread widely and became deeply rooted in north China.

riseSignals.value: Fall of Western Jin in the north (304–316).

peakPeriod.value: Former Qin under Fu Jian and his minister Wang Meng, which united the north in 376.

declineSignals.value: After the defeat at the Fei River (383), Former Qin broke apart into new kingdoms.

outcome.value: The Northern Wei (Tuoba Xianbei) conquered the last kingdom, Northern Liang, in 439.

overallCertainty.value: Known from chronicles, inscriptions and archaeology; dates and numbers are approximate.
